idiom_name: chained generator functions (one stage per generator)
implementation_notes: The documented Python idiom for a pipeline is a chain of generator functions: a generator suspends at each yield, so a stage consumes its upstream iterable and yields items one at a time with no intermediate list (docs.python.org, Functional Programming HOWTO; the itertools recipes call the same shape "data pipelines"). This replaces the classic stage-list class; for one-off value transformations the equivalent is a list of callables driven by a loop or functools.reduce, and the two can be mixed by making the last stage a terminal function.
pitfalls: Generators are single-pass: once a pipeline is consumed it cannot be re-iterated, so it must be re-created (or backed by a list) for a second pass.
A generator abandoned mid-iteration runs its finally block only when closed or garbage-collected, so files and locks opened in a stage can outlive the pipeline.
Late binding: closures created inside a loop capture the loop variable, so stage factories must bind their arguments explicitly.
